rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mountain passage follows the sky's fate; because mountains are earth's grandest and seemingly most enduring structures, their destruction depicts the fate of the whole earth and needs no further detail about lesser things.
rows.anchor: By portraying the fate of the mountains, it is as if the fate the whole earth will meet is depicted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appointed appearance of messengers is the real horror, with the preceding horrors serving as its prelude.
rows.anchor: We were never away from them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the appointed time, God summons each prophet with that prophet's people to hear whether the warning was delivered and how the people responded; 5:109 and 7:6–7 give details of this hearing.
rows.anchor: We were never away from them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form waqqitat is a customary morphological alteration of wuqqitat; the expression means that a time is appointed for the messengers.
rows.anchor: In the Arabic language, such changes in the morphological structure of a word are customary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question asks the deniers to recognize the great day for which the messengers' appearance was deferred; the answer is the Day of Judgement.
rows.anchor: appearance was deferred for the Day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question's form conveys awe: the previous question stresses the Day of Judgement, while this one stresses the judgement passed on that day.
rows.anchor: the question raised in this verse highlights the eminence of the Judgement which shall be passed on that day.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refrain states the deniers' result; despite its close connection to the preceding verse, it has an independent status in the sūrah.
rows.anchor: has been repeated in this sūrah many times and in spite of having a deep connection with its previous verse, has an independent status.

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Some take the refrain as the answer to the earlier conditional clauses; Islahi rejects this because Arabic would require the particle fa at its beginning, as in 74:8–9 and 52:9–11.
rows.anchor: Some people have regarded it to be the answer to the condition stated earlier.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The missing answer to the condition is suppressed, as in 82:1–5; this ellipsis lets the refrain recur with a distinct role at each paragraph's end.
rows.anchor: Had this been the case, this verse should have begun with the particle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Suppressing the answer makes the refrain comprehensive, and its recurrence at each paragraph's end gives it a specific status each time.
rows.anchor: at the end of each paragraph

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier destruction of Noah's people, ʿĀd, Thamūd, Lot's people, Midian, and Pharaoh's people confirms the warning: God destroyed nations that rejected their messengers, and today's criminals face the same fate.
rows.anchor: history bears witness to the fact

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An incomplete verb is suppressed; the sense is that God has persistently kept the successors of earlier wrongdoers behind them.
rows.anchor: An incomplete verb is suppressed in the verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unalterable practice shown by past destruction also confirms that the day warned of by God's messengers will certainly come.
rows.anchor: This persistent practice of the Almighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The general rule specifically warns Quraysh: if they persist in stubbornness, they will share the fate of earlier criminals, since God's law applies equally to all.
rows.anchor: their fate will be no different on the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated refrain is placed appropriately after the statement of God's practice against criminals.
rows.anchor: Its placement and occasion are absolutely clear.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word wayl encompasses every punishment criminals will face on Judgement Day; its briefness contains a horror no elaborate description can encompass.
rows.anchor: encompasses in it all forms of punishment which will be encountered by the criminals on the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After historical evidence, the passage turns to man's creation as evidence for resurrection and the Day of Judgement.
rows.anchor: The previous verses presented historical evidence. These verses present evidence drawn from the creation of man.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an argues that judgement is possible because humans were created from fluid, required by God's power, wisdom, and creativity, entailed by the provision system, and supported by innate awareness of good and evil.
rows.anchor: from the creation of man in various ways

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The initial creation of man from mud and a drop of fluid proves that resurrection is possible.
rows.anchor: By referring to man’s creation from mud and from a drop of fluid, evidence is drawn on the fact that the Day of Judgement is a possible phenomenon.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs of God's power, wisdom, and creativity in making man entail that the Day of Judgement must come.
rows.anchor: The signs of God’s power, wisdom and creativity in the creation of man entail that a Day of Judgement must come.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The elaborate system established to sustain man also entails that a Day of Judgement must come.
rows.anchor: The tremendous system for man’s sustenance elaborately set up by the Almighty also entails that a Day of Judgement must come.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Man's innate awareness of good and evil is further evidence that a Day of Judgement must come.
rows.anchor: The innate awareness about good and evil found in a person bears evidence that a Day of Judgement must come.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The initial creation of man from an insignificant fluid answers deniers who wonder how God could recreate people after their bones decay; what is already evident makes resurrection possible.
rows.anchor: when no one can deny such an obvious reality as man being created from an insignificant fluid

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mahīn means insignificant and frivolous; man comes from a trivial, ordinary fluid abundant in nature, so recreating him is not difficult.
rows.anchor: He is created from a trivial and ordinary thing found in abundance in nature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the fluid insignificant also highlights that the God who created a human from it has the power to recreate him.
rows.anchor: not powerless to re-create him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse points to the fluid's remarkable development through successive stages; qarār means a place of rest, here the womb appointed for this purpose.
rows.anchor: the fluid as it passes through various stages

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarār can mean rest or a place of rest; here it means the womb as the appointed place of safety.
rows.anchor: Here it refers to the latter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When makīn describes a place, it means secure from hazards, dangers, and undue intervention.
rows.anchor: secure from hazards, dangers and undue interventions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The secure womb holds the fluid until its appointed time, allowing its destined potential to develop; God's power then brings it out when the time expires.
rows.anchor: It is then God’s power and might which brings it out

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In fa-qadarnā, the first word is from qadr and the second from qudra.
rows.anchor: the first word is from

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Man should consider the wonders and signs of God's power in creation; those signs show that recreating man is possible for Him.
rows.anchor: when such great signs of God’s power and creativity are evident in man’s creation, then it is not impossible for Him to re-create man.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recurring warning dispels doubts about resurrection because man's own creation suffices as evidence; the deniers will see the truth and face devastation, as 37:19–21 depicts.
rows.anchor: their own creation is enough to dismiss this rejection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessings provided for human sustenance substantiate judgement: the care of humans and service of the heavens and earth entail accountability, reward for fulfilling obligations, and punishment for arrogance and ingratitude.
rows.anchor: Here the Hereafter and reward and punishment are substantiated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kifāt means gathering and bringing together.
rows.anchor: would mean “one that gathers.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form denotes something that gathers; it can function as an active subject and grammatically take an object after it.
rows.anchor: grammatically correct to bring an object

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth's providence and all-embracing nature support the Hereafter and recompense; the succeeding, counterpart sūrah develops the providence argument in more detail, at 78:6–17.
rows.anchor: arguments drawn from providence are more detailed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth gathers both living creatures and the dead; the dead remain in its custody until God orders it to release what was entrusted to it.
rows.anchor: Just as this earth embraces all living creatures, it also embraces all the dead.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dead are returned to the earth from which they were created and will be raised from it; since the earth is their original womb and retains their seed, resurrection is no more wondrous than initial creation, as 20:55 says.
rows.anchor: We have created you from the earth, and to the earth will We return you

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mountains help make the earth a cradle for human residence and upbringing, as 78:6–7 describes; 31:10 says they stabilize the earth.
rows.anchor: the mountains play a very important role

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mountain height controls clouds and winds and gathers water resources, providing sweet water; only God has the power to make these mountains.
rows.anchor: the height of these mountains is very effective in controlling the clouds and winds and in gathering natural water resources.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The provisions and signs of God's power gradually establish the Day of Judgement, so the discourse leaves its conclusion unstated and returns to the refrain against deniers.
rows.anchor: In this manner, the discourse has gradually substantiated the Day of Judgement. No need remains to mention it in words.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refrain warns those who deny despite witnessing God's providence and power that they will be devastated on Judgement Day.
rows.anchor: people who are fearless of the Day of Judgement in spite of witnessing God’s providence and power and are adamant in denying shall be devastated on that day.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The previous verse has established the Day of Judgement before the passage turns to the deniers' command to proceed to what they denied.
rows.anchor: the Day of Judgement was substantiated
